title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: nutritional considerations for single-stage ultra-marathon training and racing
authors: Tiller NB, Roberts JD, Beasley L, Chapman S, Pinto JM, et al.
journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
population: Evidence review and position stand for single-stage ultra-marathon runners
findings: Training: an individualised, periodised, food-first strategy; a moderate-to-high carbohydrate diet (about 60% of energy, 5-8 g/kg/day) to mitigate chronic glycogen depletion.
Protein of about 1.6 g/kg/day to maintain lean mass, up to 2.5 g/kg/day in demanding training.
Racing: 150-400 kcal/h (carbohydrate 30-50 g/h; protein 5-10 g/h) from calorie-dense foods; fluid 450-750 mL/h; sodium above 575 mg/L may be needed, with higher needs in heat and humidity.
Progressive gut-training and/or low-FODMAP diets are supported to relieve GI distress during racing; evidence for ketogenic diets or ketone esters is lacking; caffeine use is supported late in races.

Training: moderate-to-high carbohydrate diet (~60% of energy intake, 5-8 g/kg/day) to mitigate chronic training-induced glycogen depletion; limiting CHO before selected low-intensity sessions and/or moderating daily CHO may enhance mitochondrial function and fat oxidative capacity but may compromise high-intensity efforts.
Protein ~1.6 g/kg/day to maintain lean mass and support recovery, up to 2.5 g/kg/day may be warranted in demanding training when calorie needs are greater.

Racing: consume 150-400 kcal/h (carbohydrate 30-50 g/h; protein 5-10 g/h) from a variety of calorie-dense foods, with attention to palatability, individual tolerance and the increased preference for savoury foods in longer races.

Fluid 450-750 mL/h (~150-250 mL every 20 min); to minimise hyponatraemia likelihood electrolytes (mainly sodium) may be needed in concentrations greater than most commercial products (> 575 mg/L sodium); fluid and electrolyte requirements are elevated in hot and/or humid conditions.

Evidence supports progressive gut-training and/or low-FODMAP diets to alleviate GI distress during racing; evidence for ketogenic diets/ketone esters is lacking; strategic caffeine supports performance in the latter stages of racing, particularly when sleep deprivation may compromise safety.
limitations: Nutrition-focused, not training load; recommendations rest largely on small, low-quality ultra studies and extrapolation from shorter events; the Europe PMC abstract lists recommendations i to x.
implications: Add a fuelling-rehearsal element to long runs: practise intake in the 30-50 g/h carbohydrate (150-400 kcal/h total) range, increasing progressively, to train gut tolerance.
Show training-phase carbohydrate 5-8 g/kg/day and protein 1.6 g/kg/day as informational guidance only; the app is not a nutrition prescriber.
Frame all nutrition numbers with an individual-tolerance-first disclaimer.
Use as the ultra baseline: daily CHO 5-8 g/kg (about 60% of energy) in build weeks; protein ~1.6 g/kg, up to 2.5 g/kg in the heaviest blocks.
Race-day default 150-400 kcal/h with 30-50 g/h CHO as the tolerated floor; offer higher CHO targets only via the gut-training pathway as an athlete-selectable option.

Show fluid as a range (450-750 mL/h, scaled up in heat) never as a prescription; sodium > ~575 mg/L is a range, framed as taste/cramp support, not EAH prophylaxis (see Hew-Butler 2015/2017, Hoffman 2015).
Offer progressive gut-training in long runs and an optional low-FODMAP pre-race window for athletes who report GI symptoms.

verification.notes: Crossref (2019-01-15, 25 authors) and the complete Europe PMC abstract re-fetched; recommendations i-x all confirmed. Evidence level lowered from A to B because the position stand itself rests on low-quality evidence.
